title: LSQCA: Resource-Efficient Load/Store Architecture for Limited-Scale Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
problem: Current fault-tolerant quantum computer (FTQC) floorplan strategies devote 50% of qubit memory space to routing/overhead required for unit-time random access to all logical qubits, leaving only half the qubit count available for data storage when qubits are scarce.
motivation: The primary obstacle to practical quantum computing is the limited qubit count; existing FTQC architectures waste half of available qubits on access infrastructure rather than computation, directly halving the effective problem size that can be tackled.
method: LSQCA (Load/Store Quantum Computer Architecture) separates logical qubit memory into Computational Registers (CR), a small fast-access region, and Scan-Access Memory (SAM), a dense storage region accessed with variable latency. An instruction set is defined over these abstractions, with concrete implementations as point-SAM and line-SAM architectures. Access latency in SAM is hidden by overlapping it with other computational bottlenecks, exploiting access locality patterns identified through static analysis of quantum program memory reference timestamps. Optimization techniques leverage locality in memory reference ordering to further reduce effective latency penalties.
key_novelty: Separating quantum memory into fast Computational Registers and dense Scan-Access Memory, achieving nearly 100% memory density (vs 50% state-of-the-art) by tolerating variable-latency qubit access and hiding latency via static analysis-guided scheduling.
contributions: LSQCA floorplan architecture separating quantum memory into CR and SAM regions for nearly 100% memory density
Point-SAM and line-SAM concrete architecture designs implementing the LSQCA abstraction
Instruction set and optimization techniques exploiting access locality in quantum program memory reference timestamps
Approximately 90% memory density with only 5% execution time increase vs 50% density conventional unit-time-access floorplans

metrics.other: ~90% memory density vs ~50% for conventional FTQC floorplans; only 5% execution time increase

baselines: conventional FTQC floorplan with unit-time random access (50% memory density)
limitations: Results are based on numerical simulation of abstract qubit architectures; physical implementation constraints (qubit connectivity, gate error rates) may affect real performance.
primary_theme: load/store memory architecture for resource-efficient fault-tolerant quantum computing
